Use the `--workers` option of the `fastapi run` command. If you have more clients than what a single process can handle (for example if the virtual machine is not too big) and you have **multiple cores** in the server's CPU, then you could have **multiple processes** running with the same application at the same time, and distribute all the requests among them.[5]

```console
$ fastapi run --workers 4 main.py
```

With this setup, one Uvicorn **process manager** would listen on the **IP** and **port**, and it would start **multiple Uvicorn worker processes**.[3]

In a Dockerfile, the same option looks like this:

```dockerfile
CMD ["fastapi", "run", "app/main.py", "--port", "80", "--workers", "4"]
```

**Things to keep in mind:**

- **Memory:** multiple processes normally **don't share any memory**.[2] For example, if your code loads a Machine Learning model with **1 GB in size**, when you run one process with your API, it will consume at least 1 GB of RAM. And if you start **4 processes** (4 workers), each will consume 1 GB of RAM.[2]
- **Clusters such as Kubernetes:** If replication is already handled at the cluster level, you **would not** want to have multiple workers in the container, for example with the `--workers` command line option.[1] You would want to have just a **single Uvicorn process** per container (but probably multiple containers).[1]
- **When workers in one container make sense:** One example is when your application is **simple enough** that you can run it on a **single server**, not a cluster.[1] Another is deploying to a single server with Docker Compose.
